newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Nestle shares jump as profit soars.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nestle shares jump as profit soars.

text.p: Shares in the world's biggest food company, Nestle SA, jumped on Wednesday after it reported 1996 group net profit rose 16.6 percent to 3.40 billion Swiss francs ($2.3 billion) and proposed a big boost to its dividend.

The profit rise and planned payout of 30 francs per share were well above analysts' consensus forecast that consolidated profit would rise 10.5 percent to 3.23 billion francs and it would raise its dividend to 28 francs from 26.50.
Shares in the Vevey-based food and beverages giant ended 64 francs higher at 1,641, within hailing distance of its all-time high of 1,670 set on March 11.
Nestle had already reported 1996 sales rose 7.1 percent as volume gains teamed up with the weaker Swiss franc to boost turnover expressed in the domestic currency.

Chief financial officer Mario Corti told Reuters Financial Television the weak currency was continuing to help lift sales this year, with turnover up by double digits in Swiss franc terms in the first two months of 1997.
"Expressed in Swiss francs there is obviously very strong growth, in fact it was double-digit," Corti said. But it will be hard to maintain such growth rates for the whole year, he added.

"We have to introduce a note of caution here. It really has a lot to do with the way exchange rates behave. The Swiss franc has weakened quite a bit against most of the currencies and this will mean that the first half of this year ... will be at a level that will be hard to sustain," he said.
"It is a bit the opposite feature of what we had last year, when the first half was relatively weak and the second half obviously came in much stronger."
Corti expressed satisfaction that the 1996 gains were spread broadly across geographic areas and products.
Analysts hailed the numbers and said Nestle shares seemed set for solid gains after having lagged the blue-chip Swiss Market Index by around seven percent over the past year.

"This has not been the case for a long, long time and therefore I think the share is attractive," said Beat Wittmann at Clariden Bank, who called Nestle the best single proxy for the Swiss market as a whole.
He and other analysts were surprised Nestle put up the dividend to 30 francs, a level most expected only next year.
"I think this will have a positive impact and the share still has upside potential," Wittmann said.
Nestle said its margin on sales rose to 5.6 percent in 1996 from 5.2 percent in 1995.

The operating margin was unchanged at 9.7 percent, even though the group increased its advertising and promotional spending to support the launch of new products and increase market share, it said in a statement.

Restructuring costs also rose, mainly as a consequence of measures taken to improve competitiveness in western Europe. "They remain substantially below the level reached in the years before 1995," it said without giving details.
Corti said Nestle did not plan any major divestitures and would rely on organic growth for most of its rise in turnover.

"In contrast to some of our major competitors, we believe we are one of the most focused food companies, certainly among the large players," he said, noting only four percent of revenue came from non-food business, primarily pharmaceutical products.
Nestle will continue to review its product ranges, Corti said, but noted that it had already divested its wine business and fresh meat business in Germany.
"There is nothing (more) on the scale that I would call dramatic or really extraordinary," he added.
He reiterated that Nestle had the financial clout to review any potential acquisition opportunities that arose but intended to focus primarily on growth from within.

"We believe around two-thirds of our growth will come internally and perhaps only one-third externally, mainly to round out strategic positions that we have taken both geographically and product group-wise," he said.
-- Zurich newsroom +41 1 631 7340 ($ = 1.462 Swiss Francs)
